threads.topic: The borrowing need is shifting into housing

entries.q: The General Fund's capital financing requirement fell £21.195m this year while the HRA's rose £63.477m, taking the HRA to 44% of the total from 40%. What does the HRA business plan assume for borrowing rates over the next five years, and at what point does the 40bp HRA Project Rate discount stop covering the difference?
entries.why: New borrowing was taken at 4.65% against a book averaging 3.89%. The HRA is where the growth is, so it is where the repricing lands.

threads.topic: Running down cash instead of borrowing

entries.q: Internal borrowing rose £54.794m to £198.470m and investments closed the year at £25.384m. How much internal borrowing headroom remains before external borrowing has to resume, and what does the medium-term forecast assume it costs when it does?
entries.why: This is the right trade while investment rates sit below borrowing rates, and the council says so. It works until the cash runs out, and the year-end balance is now smaller than a single month's average.

entries.why: The council handled three calls exactly right and said publicly how it did it. The same discipline needs to hold for the remainder, and the next call dates are not in the report.

summary.text:
The best-executed treasury year we have read so far, and worth setting out because most of it is deliberate rather than lucky. Treasury came in £7.4m under budget — £4.5m on the General Fund and £2.9m on the HRA, against a £61.7m budget — and the council used the favourable position to replenish its Treasury Management Equalisation Reserve rather than spend it, which is what its own peer review had recommended.

Three LOBO lenders called during the year, and Wolverhampton rejected all three. The report explains why in terms every member can follow: lenders are calling their options and 'offering inflated long term rates deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted'. The numbers make the point — £7.0m at 3.60% was offered 6.19%, £5.0m at 4.26% was offered 6.21%, £5.0m at 4.29% was offered 6.26%. All £17.0m was repaid, leaving £13.0m of LOBOs from an opening £30.0m. The council had already built the possibility of those calls into its cashflow so it could repay without scrambling.

Alongside that, a piece of debt rescheduling: £55.8m of fixed market debt held with Barclays was repaid at a discount, projected to save over £20.0m across forty years. Between the two, most of what left the balance sheet this year was expensive money.

The direction of the balance sheet is the opposite of what we have seen elsewhere. External borrowing fell £9.064m to £870.089m while internal borrowing rose £54.794m to £198.470m — the council is deliberately running its own cash down instead of going to the market, holding investments at just £25.384m at year end. That is the right trade while investment rates sit below borrowing rates, and the report says so plainly. It is also a resource that only depletes.

The split inside the capital financing requirement is where the next question lives. The total rose £42.282m to £1,152.222m, but the General Fund share fell £21.195m while the HRA rose £63.477m — the borrowing need is now 44% housing against 40% a year ago, and rising. New borrowing was taken at an average 4.65% against a book averaging 3.89%, so every replacement pound costs more than the one it replaces.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your treasury outturn. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A note on scope first. We hold 85 PWLB loans for Wolverhampton at a balance of £857.1m. Your remaining £13.000m of LOBOs is market debt and sits outside our file, so nothing below claims to cover your whole book.

We wrote because of the LOBOs, and specifically because you published the numbers. Three lenders called during the year, you rejected all three and repaid £17.0m, and the report sets out what was actually offered: £7.0m at 3.60% offered 6.19%, £5.0m at 4.26% offered 6.21%, £5.0m at 4.29% offered 6.26%. Your own description — rates "deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted" — is the plainest statement of what is happening in that market that we have seen in a council paper.

It matters beyond Wolverhampton. We have now picked up LOBO calls at Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York and Barnet as well as your three, all within a few months, and the pattern is the same everywhere: lenders exercising options now that PWLB rates have risen far enough to make the embedded option valuable, and pricing the revised terms so the borrower walks. Almost nobody publishes the offered rate, which is why yours is useful — it puts a number on what the rest of the sector is being offered and turning down. That is a cross-council picture no single council can assemble from its own papers, and it is the kind of thing we exist to publish.

The rest of the year reads as deliberate rather than lucky, and it is worth saying so. £7.4m under budget against a £61.7m budget, with the favourable position used to replenish the Treasury Management Equalisation Reserve rather than spent — which is what your own peer review had recommended. £127.000m of new PWLB at an average 4.65%, using both the Certainty Rate and the 40bp-cheaper HRA Project Rate. Internal borrowing up £54.794m to £198.470m because cash is being run down rather than loans taken. Investments deliberately low at £25.384m and still returning 4.13% against a budget assumption of 2.10%.

Two things we can add. First, on the HRA Project Rate: it is the 40bp that most councils either do not use or use inconsistently, and we publish all three curves — standard, certainty and HRA — at both daily fixings, so the saving is visible per loan rather than reconstructed afterwards.

Second, pricing. 66 of your 85 PWLB loans sit below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, for about £114.9m of net discount against the £857.1m balance, with 19 above. We're not suggesting anything follows: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Ours is indicative and the page says so. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

For the forward requirement — £180.3m forecast for 2026-27 against the £201.1m Council approved — our monthly sector breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is thin for a year in which you may need a fifth of a billion.

On training, four fit Wolverhampton. LOBO loans (legacy) for the £13.000m still running and the option calls you have already handled well. Strategic PWLB borrowing for the certainty-versus-HRA-rate question. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. And Reporting to councillors & audit, because the way your report explains the LOBO calls is the standard we point other councils at. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
